outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the survey, highlighting the rapid evolution of LLM security threats between 2024 and 2026. It will synthesize the shift from generalized text-based vulnerabilities to highly specialized, multimodal, and inference-time exploits across four key domains: adversarial attacks on code LLMs, data/model poisoning, prompt injection, and hallucinations. The abstract will be generated last by the Assembler.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: Introduce the motivation and scope of the survey, framing the 2024-2026 period as a critical arms race between adversarial attack methodologies and defensive alignment mechanisms. Outline the transition from foundational text-based jailbreaking to complex, domain-specific threats (e.g., code generation, VLMs, RAG systems). Summarize the paper's contributions, specifically the comprehensive categorization of threats into training-time (poisoning) and inference-time (prompt injection, adversarial code attacks, hallucinations). Note: Avoid forcing specific paper citations for general claims here to prevent citation hallucination; reserve specific citations for the core sections.

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: Establish the foundational concepts and terminology for LLM security. Define key terms such as Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct vs. Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Data Poisoning. Provide a brief overview of standard LLM architectures and the standard threat model, distinguishing between white-box and black-box access, as well as training-time versus inference-time attacker capabilities. Discuss the inherent tension between model utility (e.g., functional correctness) and security alignment.

outline.title: 3. Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: Detail the evolution of data and model poisoning from 2024 to 2026. Discuss the shift from foundational text vulnerabilities to complex, multimodal backdoor attacks. Explicitly cover early 2024 techniques like implicit textual claims [Song_2024_Claim] and targeted code generation attacks [Yan_2024_LLM]. A major focus must be the critical 2024 discovery of backdoor persistence, detailing how malicious behaviors survive rigorous safety alignment processes like SFT and DPO [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Conclude with the emerging vulnerabilities in Vision-Language Models (VLMs).

outline.title: 4. Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Analyze the rapid arms race in prompt injection and jailbreaking (2024-2026). Document the strategic shift away from computationally expensive white-box gradient methods (like GCG) toward highly efficient black-box structural manipulations. Cite specific 2024 structural attacks: text flipping [Liu_2024_Flipattack], chat template manipulation [Zhao_2024_SQL], and system token injection [Zheng_2024_Improved]. Discuss the rise of automated adversarial generation using LLMs to attack LLMs, including adversarial suffixes [Kumar_2024_LLMs] and frameworks like AutoDAN [Liu_2024_Autodan]. Highlight the critical shift toward targeting RAG architectures.

outline.title: 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Models
outline.description: Examine the highly focused trajectory of adversarial attacks on specialized LLMs, particularly code generation models, between 2024 and 2025. Detail the transition from generalized jailbreaking to domain-specific exploitation of software development pipelines. Discuss exploratory vulnerability assessments [Li_2024_Exploratory, Rubel_2024_LLM] that exposed the fragility of code LLMs. Explain how traditional prompt injection adapted into stealthy transformations and comment injections to bypass safety filters [Jenko_2024_LLM, Noever_2024_AI]. Emphasize the trade-off where models optimized for functional correctness (passing unit tests) sacrifice security.

outline.title: 6. Model Reliability: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: Trace the 2024-2026 evolution of hallucination research from output-centric binary detection to granular, reasoning-aware evaluation. Discuss the 2024 surge in scalable methodologies using smaller NLI models and 7B-parameter annotators to replace expensive proprietary models [Wang_2024_Developing, Jing_2024_Scale, Gu_2024_Anah]. Highlight the paradigm shift in RAG evaluation from binary 'supported vs. unsupported' to assessing 'partial support' [Zhang_2024_Comparative, Zhang_2024_Fine]. Cover early white-box detection methods utilizing internal hidden states and SVD [Du_2024_LLM], and domain-specific applications in medical MLLMs [Asadi_2024_Deterministic].

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Provide a holistic overview of defense mechanisms designed to mitigate the threats discussed in previous sections. Cover input-level defenses (e.g., perplexity filters, guardrails, input sanitization), model-level defenses (e.g., adversarial training, robust RLHF/DPO alignment), and system-level defenses (e.g., RAG citation verification). Discuss the limitations of current alignment techniques, specifically referencing how structural manipulations and persistent backdoors can bypass standard SFT and DPO processes.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: MANDATORY dedicated section synthesizing benchmarks, datasets, metrics, and evaluation frameworks across ALL four categories. Discuss how ASR (Attack Success Rate) is measured for prompt injection and code attacks. Contrast functional unit testing with security evaluation in code LLMs. Detail the metrics used to measure backdoor persistence in poisoned models. Examine the shift in hallucination metrics from binary accuracy to granular NLI-based scoring and partial support metrics in RAG. Highlight the critical need for standardized, cross-domain evaluation frameworks that balance computational cost with accuracy.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Synthesize the gaps and limitations in the current state-of-the-art (2024-2026). Discuss the unresolved tension between model utility and security, the growing threat of multimodal and agentic vulnerabilities, and the lack of robust defenses against automated, black-box adversarial generation. Propose future research directions, emphasizing the need for reasoning-aware meta-critical evaluation frameworks and mathematically provable alignment guarantees.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: Summarize the core findings of the survey. Reiterate the rapid evolution of LLM security threats from basic text jailbreaks to sophisticated, domain-specific, and persistent attacks. Provide practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners to adopt defense-in-depth strategies that encompass data sanitization, robust alignment, and rigorous inference-time guardrails.
